objectives: The course, with an interdisciplinary approach, explores how contemporary society understand poverty and represent the poor. By focusing on the intersection of poverty and culture, the course examines how sociologists use culture as a framework to understand and address poverty. We will look at how institutions, such as family, education, and neoliberal government, shape and intervene in the lives of the poor. In light of the research done and the knowledge produced in sociology, we will read poverty narratives in popular culture, particularly in the form of literary journalism, memoir, and autobiography, and explore how life narratives and individual experiences (re)shape our understanding of poverty and the poor and (re)configure our relations with the social margin.
content: In relation to poverty narratives, the course is concerned about how upward social mobility is perceived, pursued, and achieved by individuals in life narratives. It explores how such stories of success contribute to specific knowledge about poverty and the poor, and examines how they either help or hinder the public’s understanding of the scope of the issue. We will also look at how social immobility or downward social mobility is conceived and narrated in the narratives of the homeless and the working poor to unravel the myth of social mobility. In doing so, the course attempts to explore the possibility of reconfiguring our responses to poverty and impoverished individuals.
grading_policy:
1.	Weekly attendance and participation
2.	Keeping up with the reading
3.	Three 1-2 page journals or in-class quizzes
4.	One presentation and leading group discussion
5.	One final essay
